tibetan:
གིས་སྐྱེ་བར་རྣམ་བརྟགས་པ། །རྣམ་པར་མི་མཁས་དེ་ཡི་#ནི། །རྐྱེན་ལས་བྱུང་བའི་དོན་མ་མཐོང་། །ཉོན་མོངས་ཟད་པའི་དགེ་སློང་གི །གལ་ཏེ་འཁོར་བ་རྣམ་ལྡོག་ན། །ཅི་ཕྱིར་རྫོགས་སངས་རྒྱས་རྣམས་ཀྱིས། །དེ་ཡི་རྩོམ་པ་རྣམ་མི་བཤད། །རྩོམ་#པ་ཡོད་
ན་ངེས་པར་ཡང་། །ལྟ་བར་འགྱུར་བ་ཡོངས་སུ་འཛིན། །རྟེན་ཅིང་འབྲེལ་པར་འབྱུང་བ་གང་། །དེ་ལ་སྔོན་དང་ཐ་མ་ཅི། །སྔོན་སྐྱེས་པ་ནི་ཇི་ལྟར་ན། །ཕྱི་ནས་སླར་ཡང་བཟློག་པར་འགྱུར། །སྔོན་དང་ཕྱི་མའི་མཐའ་བྲལ་བ། །འགྲོ་#བ་སྒྱུ་མ་བཞིན་དུ་སྣང་། །གང་ཚེ་སྒྱུ་མ་འབྱུང་ཞེའམ། །
གང་ཚེ་འཇིག་པར་འགྱུར་སྙམ་དུ། །སྒྱུ་མ་ཤེས་པ་དེར་མི་རྨོངས། །སྒྱུ་མ་མི་ཤེས་ཡོངས་སུ་སྲེད། །སྲིད་པ་སྨིག་རྒྱུ་སྒྱུ་འདྲ་བར། །བློ་ཡིས་མཐོང་བར་གྱུར་པ་ནི། །སྔོན་གྱི་མཐའ་འམ་ཕྱི་མའི་མཐའ། །ལྟ་བས་ཡོངས་སུ་སླད་མི་འགྱུར། །གང་དག་གིས་ནི་འདུས་བྱས་ལ། །སྐྱེ་
དང་འཇིག་པ་རྣམ་བརྟགས་པ། །དེ་དག་རྟེན་འབྱུང་འཁོར་ལོ་ཡིས། །འཁོར་ལོའི་འགྲོ་བ་རྣམ་མི་རྟོག# །དེ་དང་དེ་བརྟེན་གང་འབྱུང་#དེ། །རང་གི་དངོས་པོར་སྐྱེས་མ་ཡིན། །རང་གི་དངོས་པོ་#གང་མ་སྐྱེས། །དེ་ནི་སྐྱེ་ཞེས་ཇི་ལྟར་བྱ། །རྒྱུ་ཟད་ཉིད་ལས་ཞི་བ་ནི། །ཟད་ཅེས་བྱ་བར་རྟོག་#པ་སྟེ། །
རང་བཞིན་གྱིས་ནི་གང་མ་ཟད། །དེ་ལ་ཟད་ཅེས་ཇི་ལྟར་བརྗོད། །དེ་ལྟར་ཅི་ཡང་སྐྱེ་བ་མེད། །ཅི་ཡང་འགག་པར་མི་འགྱུར་རོ། །སྐྱེ་བ་དང་ནི་འཇིག་པའི་ལས། །དགོས་པའི་དོན་དུ་བསྟན་པའོ། །སྐྱེ་བ་ཤེས་པས་འཇིག་པ་ཤེས། །འཇིག་པ་ཤེས་པས་མི་རྟག་ཤེས། །མི་རྟག་ཉིད་ལ་འཇུག་ཤེས་
པས། །དམ་པའི་ཆོས་ཀྱང་རྟོག་#པར་འགྱུར། །གང་དག་རྟེན་ཅིང་འབྲེལ་འབྱུང་བ། །སྐྱེ་དང་འཇིག་པ་རྣམ་སྤངས་པར། །ཤེས་པར་གྱུར་པ་དེ་དག་ནི། །ལྟར་གྱུར་སྲིད་པའི་རྒྱ་མཚོ་བརྒལ། །སོ་སོའི་#སྐྱེ་བོ་དངོས་བདག་ཅན། །ཡོད་དང་མེད་པར་ཕྱིན་ཅི་ལོག །ཉེས་པས་ཉོན་མོངས་དབང་གྱུར་རྣམས། །
རང་གི་སེམས་ཀྱིས་བསླུས་པར་འགྱུར། །དངོས་ལ་མཁས་པ་རྣམས་ཀྱིས་ནི། །དངོས་པོ་མི་རྟག་བསླུ་བའི་ཆོས། །གསོག་དང་སྟོང་པ་བདག་མེད་པ། །རྣམ་པར་དབེན་ཞེས་བྱ་བར་མཐོང་། །གནས་མེད་དམིགས་པ་ཡོད་མ་ཡིན། །རྩ་བ་མེད་ཅིང་གནས་པ་མེད། །མ་རིག་རྒྱུ་ལས་ཤིན་དུ་བྱུང་། །
span:
If cyclic existence turned away
For a monk whose afflictions were exhausted,
Why would the Perfect Buddhas
Not describe its beginning?

If there were a beginning,
Then certainly views would be grasped.
How could there be a first or a last
In that which is dependently originated?

How could what has previously arisen
Be turned away again later?
The world, free from the extremes of beginning and end,
Appears like a magical illusion.

When one knows the illusion, one is not confused
By thinking, "When does the illusion arise?"
Or, "When does it perish?"
Those who do not know the illusion are completely attached to it.

When the mind sees existence
As being like a mirage or an illusion,
One is not corrupted by views
Of a beginning or an end.

Those who imagine birth and destruction
Regarding conditioned things,
Do not understand the movement of the world
According to the wheel of dependent origination.

That which arises in dependence on this or that
Has not arisen as its own inherent nature.
How can that which has not arisen
As its own inherent nature be said to "arise"?

The peace resulting from the exhaustion of causes
Is conceptualized as "exhaustion,"
But how can that which is not exhausted by nature
Be called "exhausted"?

Thus, nothing at all arises,
And nothing at all will cease.
The acts of arising and destruction
Were taught for a purposeful meaning. <note>taught as conventional truths for the sake of guiding students</note>

By knowing arising, one knows destruction;
By knowing destruction, one knows impermanence.
By knowing how to enter into impermanence itself,
One will also realize the Sublime Dharma.

Those who have come to know
Dependent origination as being
Free from arising and destruction,
Have crossed the ocean of existence.

Ordinary beings, identifying with things,
Are inverted regarding existence and non-existence.
Under the power of afflictions and faults,
They are deceived by their own minds.

Those who are skilled in the nature of things
See that things are impermanent, deceptive phenomena,
Hollow, empty, and without a self:
They see them as utterly solitary. <note>isolated from inherent existence</note>

Without a station, there is no focal point.
Without a root, they do not remain.
They arise entirely from the cause of ignorance,
tail: Completely devoid of beginning, middle, or end.
old_translation:
<meta>continues from previous page</meta>
...he who conceptualizes it as arising is unwise and has not seen the meaning of arising from conditions. 

If <term>samsara</term> <gloss>cyclic existence</gloss> were reversed for a monk whose afflictions are exhausted, why would the Perfect Buddhas not explain its beginning? 

If there were a beginning, one would certainly hold it as a view. What is the "before" or "after" of that which is dependently originated? 

How could that which arose before be reversed again later? Free from the limits of before and after, the world appears like a magical illusion. 

When one thinks "When did the illusion arise?" or "When will it perish?", one who knows the illusion is not deluded by it. One who does not know the illusion craves it. 

Those who see becoming with their intelligence as being like a mirage or a magical illusion are not defiled by views of a former limit or a later limit. 

Those who conceptualize arising and perishing in the conditioned do not understand the movement of the wheel of the wheel of dependent origination. 

Whatever arises in dependence on this or that has not arisen as its own entity. How can that which has not arisen as its own entity be said to "arise"? 

Cessation due to the exhaustion of causes is conceptualized as "exhaustion." How can that which is not exhausted by its own nature be said to have "exhausted"? 

Thus, nothing whatsoever arises, and nothing whatsoever will cease. The acts of arising and perishing were taught for a necessary purpose. 

By knowing arising, one knows perishing. By knowing perishing, one knows impermanence. By knowing how to enter into impermanence, one will realize the sacred Dharma. 

Those who have come to know dependent origination as being free from arising and perishing have crossed the ocean of becoming, which is based on views. 

Ordinary beings who grasp at entities are inverted in terms of "existence" and "non-existence." Those who are under the power of afflictions due to faults are deceived by their own minds. 

Those who are wise regarding entities see that things are impermanent, deceptive, false, empty, selfless, and isolated. 

Without a place, there is no object of perception. Being without root and without dwelling, it has arisen entirely from the cause of ignorance.
